data.name: Fix_NoSpf_What
data.value: {0} has no SPF record. SPF lists the servers that may send email for your domain. Without it, anyone can send mail that appears to come from {0}, and receiving servers are more likely to treat your real mail as spam.

data.name: Fix_NoSpf_Steps
data.value: List everything that sends email as {0}: your mail provider, newsletter and CRM tools, web shop, ticket system, and any server that sends alerts. Look up each sender's SPF include in its documentation, for example include:_spf.google.com for Google Workspace or include:spf.protection.outlook.com for Microsoft 365. Publish one TXT record on {0} that starts with v=spf1, lists those includes, and ends with ~all. Move to -all once you are sure the list is complete. A name may have only one SPF record. If one exists, merge the two instead of adding a second. Keep it to 10 DNS lookups in total, or receivers will ignore the record. Check the result with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_NoDmarc_What
data.value: {0} has no DMARC policy. DMARC tells receiving servers what to do with mail that fails the SPF and DKIM checks, and sends you reports about who sends mail as your domain. Without it, spoofed mail is accepted and you cannot see abuse.

data.name: Fix_NoDmarc_Steps
data.value: Make sure SPF and DKIM already work for all your mail, or DMARC will reject real messages later. Create a mailbox, or use a DMARC reporting service, that receives the reports. Publish a TXT record on _dmarc.{0}, starting in monitoring mode: p=none with an rua= address. Read the reports for a few weeks and fix the legitimate senders that fail. Tighten the policy step by step: p=quarantine (start with pct=25), then p=reject. Check the result with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_DmarcNone_What
data.value: The DMARC policy of {0} is p=none: mail that fails is still delivered and DMARC only reports. That is the right way to start, but it does not protect against spoofing.

data.name: Fix_DmarcNone_Steps
data.value: Read your DMARC reports (the rua address) and list the senders that fail SPF or DKIM. Fix those senders: add them to SPF, or set up DKIM signing for them. Stop senders you do not recognise. Change the policy to p=quarantine with pct=25, and raise pct to 100 over a few weeks. When nothing legitimate fails any more, move to p=reject. Add sp=reject if your subdomains do not send mail. If you deliberately stay in monitoring mode for now, mute this finding with an end date so it comes back.

data.name: Fix_NoNullMx_What
data.value: {0} has no MX record and does not appear to send mail. Without an MX, mail servers fall back to the A record of the name and try to deliver there, and nothing states that the name is not meant for mail. A null MX (RFC 7505) says so explicitly, so senders stop retrying and spoofers have one less thing to use.

data.name: Fix_NoNullMx_Steps
data.value: Check that nothing sends or receives mail as {0}. If it does, publish SPF and DMARC instead and ignore this finding. Publish one MX record with preference 0 and the exchange "." (a single dot). Also publish SPF as v=spf1 -all and a DMARC record with p=reject, if the name does not have them yet. Check the result with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_DmarcQuarantine_What
data.value: The DMARC policy that applies to {0} is p=quarantine: mail that fails SPF and DKIM goes to the spam folder instead of being refused. That is a good step, but p=reject is the goal because it stops spoofed mail from arriving at all.

data.name: Fix_DmarcQuarantine_Steps
data.value: Read your DMARC reports (the rua address) and check that nothing legitimate still fails SPF or DKIM. Raise pct to 100 if the policy still uses a lower percentage. Change the policy to p=reject. Add sp=reject if your subdomains do not send mail. If you deliberately stay on quarantine for now, mute this finding with an end date so it comes back. Check the result with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_DmarcSubdomainNotReject_What
data.value: The DMARC record that covers {0} has an sp tag that is not reject. The sp tag is the policy for every subdomain, so a weak value lets anyone send spoofed mail as a subdomain that does not exist or does not send mail.

data.name: Fix_DmarcSubdomainNotReject_Steps
data.value: List the subdomains that send mail. Each of them needs working SPF and DKIM, or its own DMARC record. Change sp= in the DMARC record of {0} to sp=reject, or remove the sp tag so that p applies to subdomains as well. Give a subdomain that must stay in monitoring mode its own _dmarc record with a weaker policy. Check the result with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_NoCaa_What
data.value: {0} has no CAA record. CAA limits which certificate authorities may issue certificates for the domain. Without it, any CA can, which makes mis-issuance harder to prevent.

data.name: Fix_NoCaa_Steps
data.value: Check which CAs issued your current certificates: see the Issuer column on the certificate list. Publish a CAA record for every CA you use, for example 0 issue "letsencrypt.org". Use issuewild for wildcard certificates. Add an iodef record with an address that should be told about refused requests. Check that your DNS provider supports CAA records (most do) and that you have not left a CA out, or its renewals will fail. Check the result with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_NoNs_What
data.value: No name server records were found for {0}. The name does not resolve, so nothing that depends on it (web, email, certificates) can work.

data.name: Fix_NoNs_Steps
data.value: Check the spelling of the name. Check that the domain is registered and has not expired: run whois and look at the status and expiry date. Check at the registrar that the domain points to the right name servers, and that those servers have a zone for {0}. Run dig NS {0} +trace to see where the chain breaks. If the domain is retired, delete or pause the asset.

data.name: Fix_DanglingCname_What
data.value: {0} is a CNAME that points to {1}, and that name does not exist. Whoever registers or claims {1} (a deleted cloud app, storage bucket or hosted service name) can serve content on {0}: a subdomain takeover.

data.name: Fix_DanglingCname_Steps
data.value: Find out what {0} was for. If it is no longer used, delete the CNAME record at your DNS provider right away. That removes the risk. If it is still needed, restore {1}: recreate the app, bucket or custom domain at the provider under the same name, or point the CNAME to the new target. Check your other records for CNAMEs that point to the same provider and may be orphaned too. In future, remove the custom domain from the provider and the DNS record together when you retire a service. Check with the commands below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_ResolverMismatch_What
data.value: Public resolvers give different answers for the {1} records of {0}. That is normal for a short while after you change a record, but it can also mean that someone changed your DNS without you knowing, or that one of your name servers serves old data.

data.name: Fix_ResolverMismatch_Steps
data.value: Look up the record with all resolvers (the lookup button below) and compare the answers. If you changed it recently, wait until the old record's TTL has passed and scan again. If it persists, ask each of your own name servers directly (see the commands below). One server with different data is the usual cause: sync or fix that zone. If an answer lists name servers or mail servers you do not recognise, treat it as a hijack: change the passwords of your registrar and DNS accounts, turn on two-factor authentication and a registry lock, and contact your registrar. If different answers are intended (split-horizon DNS), mute this finding.

data.name: Fix_DkimMissing_What
data.value: No DKIM record was found for selector {1} on {0}. DKIM signs outgoing mail so receivers can tell it really came from you. Without a published key, signed mail fails DKIM and, with it, DMARC.

data.name: Fix_DkimMissing_Steps
data.value: Check that the selector is exactly the s= value in the DKIM-Signature header of a message you sent. In your mail provider's settings, find the DKIM key or CNAME record for that selector and publish it at {1}._domainkey.{0}. Providers use either a TXT record or a CNAME. Copy the value exactly. Long keys may need to be split into several quoted strings; most DNS providers do that for you. Wait for the TTL and check with the command below. If the selector is retired, remove it from the DKIM selectors on the asset page.

data.name: Fix_DkimRevoked_What
data.value: The DKIM key of selector {1} on {0} is empty (p=), which revokes it. Mail signed with this selector fails DKIM.

data.name: Fix_DkimRevoked_Steps
data.value: If you retired the selector on purpose, remove it from the DKIM selectors on the asset page. If not, find the current public key in your mail provider's settings and publish it again at {1}._domainkey.{0}. Check that your mail system still signs with a selector that has a published key. Check with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_DkimInvalid_What
data.value: The DKIM record for selector {1} on {0} cannot be read as a public key. Receivers treat signatures with this selector as failed.

data.name: Fix_DkimInvalid_Steps
data.value: Copy the record again from your mail provider. Look for lost characters, extra spaces, or quotes inside the key. Some DNS panels limit a TXT string to 255 characters. A 2048-bit key must be split into several quoted strings. Keep the tags: v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=<key>. Check the published value with the command below, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_DkimWeak_What
data.value: The DKIM key of selector {1} on {0} is only {2} bits. Keys below 1024 bits can be broken with modest effort, which would let someone forge signed mail from your domain.

data.name: Fix_DkimWeak_Steps
data.value: In your mail provider or mail server, generate a new DKIM key of 2048 bits. Publish it under a new selector name, for example the month and year. Switch signing to the new selector and wait a few days for mail that is still in transit. Remove the old selector from DNS and from the DKIM selectors on the asset page.

data.name: Fix_DnsError_What
data.value: The DNS check for {0} could not finish: {1}. This is about the lookup, not necessarily about {0} itself.

data.name: Fix_DnsError_Steps
data.value: Check that the server running FullyQualified can reach a DNS server: run the first command there. If it cannot, check its network and the Dns:Server setting. Check that outgoing DNS (UDP and TCP port 53) is not blocked by a firewall. Compare with a public resolver (the second command). If that works, the problem is your local resolver. If every resolver answers SERVFAIL for this domain, DNSSEC may be broken or the name servers are down: run the third command and ask your DNS provider. The check tries again by itself within 15 minutes.

data.name: Fix_TlsExpired_What
data.value: The certificate of {0} expired on {1}. Browsers and apps show a security error or refuse to connect.

data.name: Fix_TlsExpiring_What
data.value: The certificate of {0} expires on {1} ({2} days left). If it is not renewed in time, visitors and systems will get security errors.

data.name: Fix_Tls_Renew_Steps
data.value: Renew the certificate now. With Let's Encrypt or another ACME client (certbot, acme.sh, win-acme, Caddy, cert-manager), run the renewal by hand and read the error. A blocked challenge (port 80, a DNS record), a changed DNS record or a rate limit are the usual causes. With a commercial certificate, request a replacement at your reseller or CA and complete the validation. Install the new certificate everywhere this name is served: web server or IIS binding, load balancer, Azure Key Vault with Application Gateway or Front Door, CDN, Java keystore. Then reload the service. Check the result with the command below: the dates and the issuer should be new. Automate it. Certificate lifetimes are getting shorter (100 days in 2027, 47 days in 2029), so renewing by hand will not stay manageable. If the system is retired, pause or delete the asset instead.

data.name: Fix_TlsTrust_What
data.value: The certificate that {0} presents is not trusted ({2}). Browsers and apps will warn visitors or refuse to connect.

data.name: Fix_TlsTrust_Mismatch_Title
data.value: The certificate does not cover the name

data.name: Fix_TlsTrust_Mismatch_Steps
data.value: The certificate is valid for: {1}. {0} is not among those names. If {0} should be served by this certificate, reissue it with {0} as a subject alternative name, or use a wildcard certificate that covers it. If the server hosts several sites, check that it picks the right certificate for {0} (SNI or virtual host settings) and that the default certificate is not served instead. If {0} points to the wrong server, fix the A, AAAA or CNAME record: look it up with the button below.

data.name: Fix_TlsTrust_Chain_Title
data.value: The certificate chain is not trusted

data.name: Fix_TlsTrust_Chain_Steps
data.value: A missing intermediate certificate is the most common cause: install the full chain (for example fullchain.pem), not only the server certificate. A self-signed certificate, or one from a private CA, is not trusted by browsers. Use a certificate from a public CA. For internal systems, make sure the clients trust your CA and mute this finding. Check that no certificate in the chain has expired, including the intermediate ones. Check the chain with the second command (it prints every certificate), reload the service, then scan again.

data.name: Fix_TlsError_What
data.value: The TLS check could not connect to {0} on port {1}: {2}. Nothing was checked, so the state of the certificate is unknown.

data.name: Fix_TlsError_Steps
data.value: Check that the address and port are right. An endpoint is written as host:port, and without a port 443 is used. Check that the service runs and listens on that port (the first command), and that no firewall blocks the connection from the server running FullyQualified. If the name does not resolve, fix or add the DNS record. If the connection works but the handshake fails, the server may only support old protocols (TLS 1.0 or 1.1) or share no cipher suite with this client. Enable TLS 1.2 or higher. If it says the host is not allowed, this installation blocks private addresses: set Scanning:AllowPrivateAddresses to true, or use a public name. If it is not meant to be reachable, pause the asset or make the check optional.

data.name: Fix_CtError_What
data.value: The certificate log search for {0} failed: {1}. The public services that list certificates (crt.sh, then Cert Spotter) were both unavailable. Nothing is wrong with your domain, and nothing is monitored differently because of it.

data.name: Fix_CtError_Steps
data.value: Wait a little: crt.sh is a free service that is often overloaded or rate limiting, and the search falls back to Cert Spotter when crt.sh fails. Then press Find subdomains again. If it keeps failing for hours, check that the server running FullyQualified can reach https://crt.sh and https://api.certspotter.com (outgoing HTTPS, proxy, firewall). Very large domains can time out. Add the important hostnames as assets yourself instead. You do not need this search to monitor a domain: it only helps to find hostnames you did not know about.
